name: Metformin (Glucophage)
summary: Metformin is a diabetes medication that psychiatrists commonly use off-label to help prevent or treat antipsychotic-related weight gain. It’s not a stimulant and it doesn’t “melt fat,” but it can help slow weight creep, reduce insulin resistance, and make weight management more realistic—especially early.
description: Metformin is best known for type 2 diabetes, but in psychiatry it’s often used off-label to prevent or reduce weight gain from antipsychotics (like olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, clozapine). It’s usually started low and increased slowly to avoid stomach side effects. The rare but serious risk is lactic acidosis—especially in people with kidney problems, severe dehydration, heavy alcohol use, or low-oxygen medical states. It can also lower vitamin B12 over time, which matters because B12 deficiency can look like depression, brain fog, and neuropathy. The goal is usually to plateau weight gain and improve metabolic labs—not to create rapid weight loss.
patient_summary: In psych care, metformin is used off-label to help stop antipsychotic weight gain from running away. Think: “put the brakes on” rather than “instant weight loss.” Most people notice the biggest change over weeks to months. The main downside is GI stuff (diarrhea, nausea), especially if you increase too fast or use immediate-release without food. The rare scary risk is lactic acidosis—most relevant if kidney function is low, you’re dehydrated, you drink heavily, or you’re medically unstable.

linked_conditions.context: Common off-label strategy in psychiatry to prevent or reduce weight gain and metabolic risk from antipsychotics. Early use is often aimed at stopping the upward trajectory (plateau), but some patients also lose weight over time.
Not used to treat insomnia. Any sleep changes are usually indirect (eg, improved energy from better metabolic health, or GI upset disrupting sleep).
Not an anxiolytic. It does not treat anxiety directly.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to metformin or any component
Acute or chronic metabolic acidosis (including diabetic ketoacidosis)

efficacy_response.metric: Weight-gain plateau or modest weight loss over months (psychiatric off-label use)
efficacy_response.comparison_data: Most effective when started early and titrated as tolerated; benefits are modest rather than dramatic
efficacy_response.patient_text: In psych care, metformin usually helps by slowing or stopping antipsychotic weight gain and improving insulin resistance. It’s not a quick fix, but it can shift the trend in the right direction over weeks to months—especially if you start it early instead of waiting for large weight gain.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Food decreases and delays absorption; taking with meals improves tolerability
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Metabolic effect builds over days; maximum effect may take up to 2 weeks
pharmacokinetics.duration_XR: Metabolic effect builds over days; maximum effect may take up to 2 weeks
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food reduces GI upset; ER is typically taken with the evening meal

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: In psychiatry, metformin is used off-label to prevent or treat antipsychotic-related weight gain and metabolic problems. The goal is usually to slow weight gain (plateau it) and improve insulin resistance—not to create rapid weight loss.
items: {link:condition:antipsychotic-induced-weight-gain:Antipsychotic-induced weight gain}: Prevention and treatment, especially with higher-risk antipsychotics
Metabolic risk support: Insulin resistance, rising fasting glucose/A1c, or increasing waist circumference while on antipsychotics
off_label: Early-intervention strategy when starting an antipsychotic associated with significant weight gain risk
Adjunct to lifestyle changes when weight is trending up despite reasonable effort

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: This is what patients commonly describe when metformin is used for antipsychotic weight gain in real life:

quotes: It didn’t make weight fall off, but it stopped the steady climb.
I finally felt like my weight wasn’t sprinting ahead of me anymore.
It’s subtle—more like the scale stopped creeping up.
items.note: The most realistic goal is plateau of weight gain. Some people do lose weight, but it’s usually gradual.

quotes: The diarrhea was real at first—going up too fast was a mistake.
If I take it with food and ramp slowly, it’s totally manageable.
The XR version was way easier on my stomach.
items.note: GI symptoms are the main reason people quit. Slow titration and taking with meals helps a lot.

quotes: I felt less sluggish after a few weeks—like my body wasn’t fighting me as much.
My sugar cravings calmed down a bit, which surprised me.
Not a mood med, but I felt more stable physically.
items.note: These experiences are often indirect effects of improved metabolic control and/or less weight acceleration.

quotes: A year in, my labs showed low B12—now I supplement and feel clearer.
I thought I was getting depressed again, but it was B12-related fatigue.
Nobody told me to watch B12. I wish we checked it sooner.
items.note: B12 deficiency can show up as fatigue, cognitive fog, low mood, or neuropathy—so it matters in psych patients.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Metformin isn’t a “take it and feel it in an hour” medication. It works in the background by shifting metabolism over time.
key_points: Within days: Metabolic effects begin (especially on fasting glucose/insulin resistance)
Up to ~2 weeks: Maximum metabolic effect ramps in
Weeks to months: The weight trajectory changes (plateau or modest loss)
IR peaks in 2-3 hours; ER peaks in 6-8 hours, but the clinical benefit is about consistent daily use, not peak effect

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.comparison: Weight gain continues without intervention in many patients
sections.text: In psychiatric practice, metformin is commonly used because it can reduce the slope of weight gain from antipsychotics and improve metabolic labs. The effect is usually modest, and it’s strongest when started early and titrated to a tolerated target dose.
sections.clinical_details: Metformin’s benefit in antipsychotic-associated weight gain is best framed as metabolic support: improved insulin sensitivity and a reduced tendency toward ongoing gain. Patients often see the biggest difference when metformin is paired with realistic lifestyle interventions and when the titration is slow enough to keep GI side effects from forcing discontinuation.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Rare but life-threatening: metformin-associated lactic acidosis—higher risk with kidney impairment, severe dehydration, heavy alcohol use, or low-oxygen medical states.
sections.black_box: Postmarketing cases of metformin-associated lactic acidosis have resulted in death and severe cardiovascular instability. Symptoms can be subtle (malaise, muscle aches, sleepiness, abdominal pain, shortness of breath). If suspected, stop metformin and seek urgent hospital care; hemodialysis may be needed.
other: Kidney function matters: do not use if eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2
Hold metformin during acute illness with dehydration, severe vomiting/diarrhea, or suspected acute kidney injury
Temporarily hold around iodinated contrast in higher-risk situations (especially AKI or low eGFR) and restart only after kidney function is stable
Surgery/procedures: commonly held the day of surgery and resumed when stable and eating with acceptable renal function
Long-term use can lower vitamin B12 and contribute to anemia or neuropathy
patient_counseling: Take with food. If you rush the dose increases, your GI tract will punish you.

Know the red flags for lactic acidosis: unusual extreme fatigue, muscle pain, belly pain, fast breathing/shortness of breath, confusion, feeling very sleepy or “not right.” Don’t power through—get urgent care.
Avoid heavy alcohol intake. Alcohol + metformin + dehydration is a bad combo.
If you’re sick with vomiting/diarrhea or you can’t keep fluids down, hold metformin and contact your clinician.
Ask about kidney labs (eGFR) and vitamin B12 monitoring, especially if you’ve been on it for years or you have neuropathy or fatigue.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: GI side effects (diarrhea, nausea, abdominal discomfort). Long-term: vitamin B12 deficiency. Rare but serious: lactic acidosis (highest risk with kidney impairment or severe illness).
plain_language_list: Low vitamin B12 over time (can cause fatigue, numbness/tingling, anemia)

common.incidence: >10% (rates vary by formulation; higher with IR, lower with ER)
common.patient_note: This is the headline side effect. It’s usually worst at the start or after dose increases. Taking with meals, going slow, and switching to extended-release can make a huge difference.
Often improves after a few weeks. If you’re miserable, the usual fix is slower titration, taking it with food, or using ER.
Can happen early or with dose jumps. If symptoms persist, reassess dose, formulation, and other GI contributors.
Sometimes it’s transient. If fatigue is persistent months in, think about B12 (and anemia) rather than blaming your brain.

common.incidence: Reported; risk increases with duration and higher doses
common.patient_note: B12 deficiency can look like depression, brain fog, and neuropathy. It’s reversible when caught. This is why periodic B12 checks matter.

serious: Metformin-associated lactic acidosis: rare but life-threatening; can present with malaise, muscle aches, abdominal pain, sleepiness, shortness of breath, hypotension, and bradyarrhythmias. Higher risk with kidney impairment, hypoxic medical states (shock, sepsis, acute heart failure/MI), severe dehydration, heavy alcohol use, hepatic impairment, and certain interacting medications. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Severe dehydration/acute kidney injury during illness: can increase metformin levels and lactic acidosis risk; hold medication and seek care if significantly ill.
Hepatotoxicity: rare case reports; jaundice, fatigue, elevated liver enzymes—stop medication and evaluate.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Most metformin interaction risk in psych practice is about lactic acidosis risk, kidney stress, or acid-base balance—not serotonin syndrome or QT issues.

items.risk: Increased risk of metabolic acidosis and metformin-associated lactic acidosis, especially in higher-risk patients.
items.action: Use caution. Consider closer monitoring (renal function, symptoms of acidosis) and avoid risky combos in medically fragile patients.

items.risk: Contrast-associated acute kidney injury can reduce metformin clearance and increase lactic acidosis risk.
items.action: Temporarily withhold metformin in higher-risk situations (eg, AKI, eGFR <30; some clinicians are more conservative with lower eGFR or additional risk factors). Recheck kidney function ≥48 hours after contrast and restart only if stable.

items.with: Alcohol (especially heavy use or binge drinking)
items.risk: Alcohol can increase lactate production and worsen dehydration, raising lactic acidosis risk.
items.action: Avoid heavy alcohol intake. If alcohol use is significant, reassess whether metformin is appropriate and emphasize hydration and sick-day rules.

items.with: Medications that worsen kidney function or cause significant hemodynamic changes (eg, severe dehydration from diuretics in vulnerable patients)
items.risk: Reduced metformin clearance and higher lactic acidosis risk if kidney function drops.
items.action: Use caution in high-risk patients. Reinforce holding metformin during acute illness, dehydration, or AKI risk.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Metformin does not cause dependence, withdrawal, or rebound anxiety. You typically do not need to taper it. If you stop it, the main risk is that weight and metabolic markers may drift back in the wrong direction over time—especially if the antipsychotic is still on board.
key_points: No withdrawal syndrome: stopping does not cause seizures, delirium, or rebound psychiatric symptoms
If stopping due to GI side effects, consider switching to ER or slowing titration instead of quitting entirely
If stopping due to illness risk (dehydration/AKI), it’s often held temporarily and resumed when stable
If stopping because the antipsychotic was changed or discontinued, reassess weight/metabolic trend over the next few months

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Psychiatry use is off-label and usually aimed at preventing or reducing antipsychotic weight gain. Start low, go slow, and take it with meals. If the stomach can’t tolerate it, extended-release is often the move.

adult.antipsychotic_weight_gain_ir_initial: 500 mg PO once daily with a meal OR 500 mg PO BID with meals
adult.antipsychotic_weight_gain_ir_titration: Increase by 500 mg/day every 1 to 2 weeks based on tolerability and response
adult.antipsychotic_weight_gain_ir_target: 1,000 mg PO BID (2,000 mg/day total) if tolerated
adult.antipsychotic_weight_gain_er_initial: 500 mg PO once daily with the evening meal
adult.antipsychotic_weight_gain_er_titration: Increase by 500 mg/day every 1 to 2 weeks based on tolerability and response
adult.antipsychotic_weight_gain_er_target: 2,000 mg PO once daily if tolerated
adult.renal_adjustment: eGFR ≥60: no adjustment; eGFR 45 to <60: no adjustment but monitor more often; eGFR 30 to 45: initiation generally not recommended (some experts start 500 mg nightly and titrate cautiously); if continuing, max ~500 mg BID with close monitoring; eGFR <30: contraindicated
adult.hepatic_adjustment: Avoid in severe hepatic impairment; liver disease increases lactic acidosis risk. If mild/moderate impairment, use caution and monitor closely—especially if other lactic-acid–producing risks are present
adult.older_adults: Start conservatively and titrate slowly due to higher likelihood of reduced renal function; ensure eGFR is appropriate and monitor regularly

sections.simple_explanation: For psychiatry, the dosing strategy is boring on purpose: start low, increase slowly, and take it with food. The goal is to keep people on it long enough to actually get benefit without getting chased off by GI side effects.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: In psych practice, the most relevant special-population issues are kidney function (especially in older adults), medical instability (dehydration, sepsis, hypoxia), and long-term B12 monitoring. Pregnancy and breastfeeding decisions are individualized and often managed alongside OB and endocrine care.
sections.pregnancy: Metformin crosses the placenta. In psychiatry, it’s not typically prescribed specifically for weight gain during pregnancy; decisions about continuing metformin are usually driven by diabetes/GDM/PCOS management and pregnancy-specific risks/benefits. Avoid use in pregnant patients who are at risk for intrauterine growth restriction, preeclampsia, or significant medical instability per guideline-based care.
sections.lactation: Metformin is present in breast milk in low amounts; reported relative infant doses are generally well below typical safety thresholds in available studies. Breastfeeding decisions should consider infant exposure, maternal benefit, and alternative options.
sections.geriatrics: Higher risk of renal impairment and dehydration-related complications. Start low, titrate slowly, monitor eGFR more frequently, and reinforce sick-day rules (hold during significant illness, dehydration, or AKI risk).
sections.hepatic: Liver disease increases lactic acidosis risk because the liver clears lactate. Avoid in severe hepatic impairment and be cautious in moderate impairment, especially if other risk factors exist (alcohol use, dehydration, hypotension, sepsis, reduced cardiac function, reduced kidney function).
sections.renal: Renal function drives safety. Contraindicated if eGFR <30. Increased monitoring is recommended when eGFR is <60, and initiation is generally avoided at eGFR 30-45 unless a cautious expert plan is used.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Weight and waist circumference: baseline and follow-up (trend matters more than a single number)
Metabolic labs: fasting glucose and/or HbA1c as clinically appropriate; lipid profile based on overall metabolic risk and antipsychotic monitoring protocols
Renal function (eGFR): before starting; at least annually; more often (every 3-6 months) if eGFR <60 or if risk factors are present
Vitamin B12: periodic monitoring (commonly every 1-2 years, sooner if anemia, neuropathy, fatigue, or cognitive symptoms)
GI tolerability: diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain—especially during titration; adjust pace or switch to ER if needed
Lactic acidosis vigilance in high-risk situations: acute illness, severe dehydration, hypoxic states, heavy alcohol intake, declining kidney function, interacting medications (eg, topiramate)

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Formulation choice is mostly about tolerability. Extended-release is often easier on the stomach, which matters if you’re using metformin long-term for antipsychotic metabolic effects.
items: Immediate-release tablets: 500 mg, 850 mg, 1,000 mg (generic available)
Extended-release tablets (various ER products): 500 mg, 750 mg, 1,000 mg (generic available; swallow whole)
Oral solution: 500 mg/5 mL (useful for people who can’t swallow tablets; some products contain excipients like propylene glycol depending on formulation)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Metformin lowers hepatic glucose production, reduces intestinal glucose absorption, and improves insulin sensitivity (better peripheral glucose uptake and utilization). In psych patients, that matters because antipsychotics can push the body toward insulin resistance and fat storage—metformin helps counter that metabolic drift.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: For antipsychotic weight gain, metformin is one of the most commonly used off-label meds because it’s familiar, generally safe when kidney function is adequate, and it targets the metabolic side of the problem. It works best as an early intervention (before weight gain becomes entrenched), alongside realistic nutrition and activity changes, and with ongoing monitoring of weight and metabolic labs. If weight gain is severe or metabolic markers worsen despite metformin, clinicians may reassess the antipsychotic choice/dose and consider additional metabolic strategies.

seo.title: Metformin for Antipsychotic Weight Gain: Dosing, Side Effects, and Safety
seo.description: Metformin in psychiatry: off-label use for antipsychotic-related weight gain and metabolic risk. How it works, dosing (IR vs ER), GI side effects, vitamin B12 deficiency, lactic acidosis risk, interactions, and monitoring.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.q: Why would a psychiatrist prescribe metformin?
faqs.a: Mostly for antipsychotic-related weight gain and metabolic risk. If an antipsychotic is helping your symptoms but your weight and labs are drifting the wrong way, metformin is one of the most common off-label tools to slow that trend.

faqs.q: Will metformin make me lose weight?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but the more realistic goal is that it slows or stops ongoing weight gain from the antipsychotic. If weight loss happens, it’s usually modest and gradual over weeks to months—not a dramatic drop.

faqs.q: How long until metformin helps with antipsychotic weight gain?
faqs.a: Metabolic effects begin within days, but the weight trend usually shows change over weeks to months. It’s a “background” medication—you don’t feel it kick in like an anxiety med.

faqs.q: What’s the difference between metformin IR and XR?
faqs.a: XR (extended-release) is often easier on the stomach and is usually taken once daily with the evening meal. IR (immediate-release) can work fine too, but it’s more likely to cause diarrhea and is often taken once or twice daily with meals.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: GI issues: diarrhea, nausea, stomach upset, gas/bloating—especially at the beginning or when the dose increases too fast. Taking it with food and titrating slowly helps a lot. XR is often better tolerated.

faqs.q: What is lactic acidosis and should I be scared?
faqs.a: It’s rare, but it’s serious. The risk goes up if kidney function is low, you’re severely dehydrated, you have a low-oxygen medical state (like sepsis/shock), or you drink heavily. Symptoms can be vague—extreme fatigue, muscle pain, belly pain, fast breathing/shortness of breath, feeling unusually sleepy or confused. If that happens, stop metformin and get urgent medical care.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper metformin?
faqs.a: No. Metformin doesn’t cause dependence or withdrawal. If you stop it, the main issue is that weight/metabolic markers may drift back up over time—especially if you’re still on the same antipsychotic.

faqs.q: Does metformin affect mood or anxiety directly?
faqs.a: No—metformin isn’t an antidepressant or anti-anxiety medication. Any mood improvements people notice are usually indirect (feeling physically better, less metabolic sluggishness, less distress about weight gain).

faqs.q: Why do you monitor vitamin B12 with metformin?
faqs.a: Long-term metformin can lower B12. Low B12 can look like depression or burnout (fatigue, brain fog), and it can also cause neuropathy (numbness/tingling). Catching it early is easy—labs and supplementation if needed.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol on metformin?
faqs.a: Light alcohol may be fine for some people, but heavy alcohol use is a problem because it increases lactic acidosis risk—especially if you’re dehydrated or medically unwell. If alcohol use is significant, talk with your clinician before starting or continuing metformin.

faqs.q: When should I temporarily stop metformin?
faqs.a: Common ‘hold’ situations include severe vomiting/diarrhea or dehydration, suspected acute kidney injury, or certain higher-risk contrast imaging or surgical situations (based on your kidney function and overall risk). If you’re not sure, ask your clinician—this is one place where playing it safe is smart.
